newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria far right sees new EU conservative pact.
newsitem.headline: Austria far right sees new EU conservative pact.

text.p: Austrian far-right leader Joerg Haider said his party's strong showing in European parliamentary elections on Sunday would trigger a realignment of conservative groups in the Strasbourg-based legislature.
The Freedom Party (FPOe) scored an all-time high in Sunday's poll, winning 28 percent of the vote and securing seven of Austria's 21 seats in the European Parliament.
Haider, 46, swiftly opened the way for an alliance with like-minded groups and said the FPOe would use its new-found muscle to press for a revision of the Maastricht treaty.
"We are against Maastricht and we will join with all members of the European Parliament who think the same way," Haider, FPOe chief for the past 10 years, told reporters.

The FPOe campaigned for the Alpine republic's first EU vote on an "Austria first" platform. It has been a vocal opponent of European economic and monetary union and has called for a cut in big net payments to Brussels.
"We want to reform Maastricht. We want a Europe of the fatherlands, one that gives power to the people," said Haider.
Austria joined the EU on a wave of euphoria on January 1, 1995. Since then, rising unemployment and record insolvencies have soured the public's perception of the bloc.

Haider said the FPOe, the most successful far right group in Europe, had already received numerous offers from sympathetic groups in the European assembly and forecast cooperation talks would begin almost immediately.
Austrian media have reported that factions within Britain's ruling Conservative Party and Italy's Northern League have already made overtures to the FPOe.
British conservatives are split over Britain's future in Europe and separatist Northern League leader Umberto Bossi has called for a revision of the Maastricht treaty.
A top FPOe candidate in Sunday's vote forecast that the party would strike a coalition agreement with European conservatives by the end of the year.
"I can tell you that several conservative parties were just waiting for this result to start discussions," said Peter Sichrovsky, the party's number two candidate.
Sichrovsky, a Jewish journalist and author whose parents fled Austria during World War Two, defended the FPOe's political credentials and rejected the far-right tag.
"All the people who wanted to push the Freedom Party into a far-right corner have to recognise it is a conservative party like any other in Europe," he told reporters.

Sichrovsky, 50, was once a fierce critic of Haider. In 1991, when the then governor of Carinthia praised Adolf Hitler's employment policies, Sichrovsky compared him with "the scum that floats to the top, even when you add fresh water".
Haider was forced to resign over the comments. But the nationalist leader has toned down his rhetoric, focusing more on the government's failure to stem rising unemployment.
The far right on Sunday emerged as the biggest party in the provinces of Carinthia, Salzburg and Tyrol for the first time.
